title: Runtime shard splitting with kernel-aware steering for latency-first QoS
creator: Priya Nair
description:
Background: Our prefill/decode pipeline currently groups work primarily by token-phase windows which optimizes throughput but can create long-tail latency for latency-sensitive traffic. Kernel selection today is chosen per-microbatch without explicit steering for latency-critical requests. We need a scheduling policy that prioritizes latency-sensitive requests while still maintaining reasonable throughput and kernel utilization across heterogeneous hardware and model variants.

Problem statement: Latency-first customer routes (web search, chat UI) are experiencing tail latency increases during mixed workloads because: (1) large decode-heavy prefill jobs monopolize kernels optimized for throughput, (2) attention-heavy long-context prefill phases increase memory pressure causing suboptimal kernel choices, and (3) our phase grouping lacks an escape hatch to split shards when headroom is low. We also want fairness between paying customers and internal workloads without regressing cost targets.

Proposal summary: Implement a "runtime shard splitting + kernel-aware steering" policy that: (a) tags incoming requests with QoS (latency-first | balanced | throughput) and attention-cost hints (estimated KV size, attention flops estimate), (b) opportunistically splits large phases into shards when predicted completion time would violate latency SLO for in-flight latency-first requests, and (c) steers shards to kernels optimized for the desired latency/throughput tradeoff. The policy uses a lightweight estimator to predict kernel execution time per shard and picks splitting points that minimize tail latency while preserving overall token throughput.

Design details: 
- Request tagging: extend the routing layer to propagate QoS and attention-cost metadata. QoS is set by API route or user config; attention-cost is estimated from input length and model profile.
- Shard heuristic: for prefill phases longer than X ms expected on the preferred kernel and with at least Y concurrent latency-first requests, split into N shards where N is proportional to the predicted tail contribution. Shard boundaries prefer contiguous token regions that preserve attention locality to keep KV reuse efficient.
- Kernel-aware steering: maintain microbenchmarks for each kernel variant (FP16/INT8 fused attention kernels, sparse-optimized kernels) per model and sequence length. Use these to compute per-shard expected latency and choose the kernel that hits the QoS target with minimal throughput loss. If the chosen kernel cannot be scheduled within the latency window, fall back to hedged execution across two kernels (hedge window configurable).
- Fairness: introduce a proportional capacity cap for latency-first routes so shards do not starve throughput-tier work. Use a simple weighted token budget allocator that charges shards heavier for latency-first tags during high contention.
- Metrics and probing: instrument per-shard scheduler events, chosen kernel, estimated vs observed latency, and KV reuse ratio. Add alerts for shard-split churn and kernel mispredictions.

Acceptance criteria: 
- Latency-first 95th percentile reduces by at least 20% in mixed-workload synthetic replay compared to baseline (same or better than canary).
- Overall token throughput drops by <5% in steady-state mixed workload.
- Kernel selection accuracy >85% (measured as chosen kernel finishing within 1.2x predicted latency).
- No increase in error rates or token corruption.
- Feature gated and rolloutable by route or org.

Risks and mitigations: 
- Kernel misprediction causing oscillation: mitigate with conservative backoff and smoothing of kernel performance signals.
- KV cache fragmentation: choose shard boundaries that preserve contiguous KV segments and run offline microbenchmarks to measure cache hit impacts.
- Increased scheduler complexity: keep the initial implementation as a policy layer that uses existing allocator primitives; avoid deep runtime changes on first pass.

Test plan: 
- Unit tests for QoS tagging and shard boundary selection heuristics.
- Microbenchmarks across kernels with representative model sizes and sequence lengths.
- Synthetic mixed-workload replay (latency-first + throughput-heavy) in staging with production-like traffic shapes.
- Gradual canary rollout by route with circuit-breaker that disables shard splitting on regressions.

Rollout plan: 
1) Feature flag gated implementation in runtime-1.20 behind a config flag per-deployment.
2) Staging integration tests + perf benchmarks.
3) Canary by org for small cohorts (5% traffic) with observability dashboard.
4) Expand to 25% then full rollout if metrics meet acceptance criteria.

Related artifacts: design doc (https://docs.internal.redwood.com/runtime/shard-splitting-design), perf dashboards (https://grafana.redwood.com/d/abcd123/shard-splitting-experiments), prototype PR (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2418).
